title: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH DAVID’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP BEFORE ISRAEL
paragraphs: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH DAVID’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP BEFORE ISRAEL

David committed his sin in secret. Years later, his own son turned a rooftop into a public declaration of rebellion. But buried beneath one of the darkest scandals in the Bible is a terrifying warning about sin—and an astonishing reason sinners can still run to Jesus.
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stare at the page and whisper...
“God actually allowed this story to remain in Scripture?”
Second Samuel 16 is one of them.
A king is running for his life.
A son has betrayed his father.
A trusted counselor has become an architect of rebellion.
Ten women have been left behind in a palace that is about to fall into enemy hands.
And then someone carries a tent onto a rooftop.
Not just any rooftop.
David’s rooftop.
And what happens there is so shameful that many Christians can read through the story of David for years without stopping long enough to understand why this horrifying scene matters.
Because this was not merely about sex.
It was about a throne.
It was about rebellion.
It was about humiliation.
It was about consequences.
And, when we follow the biblical story all the way through, it forces us to confront a truth we desperately need:
God can forgive sin completely without pretending sin was harmless.
David had once stood at the summit of Israel.
The shepherd boy nobody expected became the giant killer nobody could ignore.
The fugitive became king.
The songwriter became warrior.
The forgotten son became the man Scripture describes as a man after God's own heart.
But being used by God never made David incapable of falling.
One evening, David was walking on the roof of his palace when he saw Bathsheba.
That rooftop became connected to one of the darkest chapters of his life.
Desire became action.
Action became concealment.
Concealment became manipulation.
And manipulation eventually became bloodshed.
Uriah died.
David's secret remained hidden from human eyes for a time.
But never from God's.
Then Nathan the prophet walked into David's world carrying a message no crown could silence.
“You are the man.”
And the Lord announced consequences that would reach into David's own household.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 is chilling:
כִּי אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר ... נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנֶגֶד הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Ki attah asita basater ... neged kol-Yisrael weneged hashemesh.
The sense is:
“You did it secretly ... [but this will occur] before all Israel and before the sun.”
David had hidden his sin.
God was telling him that the consequences would not remain hidden.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Years pass.
David's family begins tearing itself apart.
Amnon violates Tamar.
Absalom burns with anger.
Amnon dies at Absalom's command.
Absalom becomes estranged from David.
Eventually the handsome, charismatic prince begins stealing the hearts of Israel.
Then rebellion erupts.
David—the giant killer, warrior, king—is forced to flee Jerusalem because his own son wants his throne.
Imagine that walk.
David once entered Jerusalem as king.
Now he leaves it weeping.
The crown is still his, but the city is slipping from his hands.
Second Samuel 15 tells us that David fled with his household but left ten concubines behind to care for the palace.
Ten women.
Remember them.
Because biblical scandals are often told through famous men's names while nearly forgotten people bear terrible consequences in the background.
Absalom enters Jerusalem.
David is gone.
The palace is his.
But taking a palace is not enough.
Absalom needs Israel to believe there will be no reconciliation between father and son.
That is when Ahithophel gives him horrifying advice.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 16:21 begins:
בּוֹא אֶל־פִּלַגְשֵׁי אָבִיךָ
Bo el-pilagshei avikha.
“Go in to your father's concubines.”
Why?
Ahithophel explains that when Israel hears what Absalom has done, everyone will know the rupture with David is complete.
Then comes verse 22:
וַיַּטּוּ לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם הָאֹהֶל עַל־הַגָּג וַיָּבֹא אַבְשָׁלוֹם אֶל־פִּלַגְשֵׁי אָבִיו לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayyattu le-Avshalom ha'ohel al-haggag, vayyavo Avshalom el-pilagshei aviv le'einei kol-Yisrael.
They spread a tent for Absalom “on the roof,” and Absalom went in to his father's concubines “before the eyes of all Israel.”
There it is.
עַל־הַגָּג — al-haggag.
“On the roof.”
And:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — le'einei kol-Yisrael.
“Before the eyes of all Israel.”
The biblical text does not describe the women's thoughts, words, or consent, so we should not manufacture details Scripture does not give us.
But Scripture leaves no doubt about Absalom's purpose.
These women were being drawn into a public political act designed to disgrace David and demonstrate Absalom's irreversible rejection of his father.
The bedroom had become propaganda.
Sex had become a declaration of power.
The rooftop had become a stage.
And Israel was the audience.
Now remember Nathan's words.
David had sinned בַסָּתֶר — basater.
“In secret.”
But the consequences would unfold:
נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — neged kol-Yisrael.
“Before all Israel.”
Then years later, the narrator describes Absalom's rooftop scandal:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — le'einei kol-Yisrael.
“Before the eyes of all Israel.”
The connection is difficult to miss.
What David tried to bury had consequences that eventually walked into daylight.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been hiding.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your parents don't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your friends see your Bible verses, your Sunday smile, your worship playlist, your Christian posts...
but they don't see what happens when the door closes.
They don't see the messages.
They don't see the addiction.
They don't see the browser history.
They don't hear the bitterness.
They don't know about the relationship.
They don't know what happened years ago.
They don't know the compromise you have renamed “struggling” because calling it sin would require you to confront it.
And perhaps you have mistaken secrecy for safety.
David's story destroys that illusion.
Sin does not become harmless because nobody applauds it, photographs it, exposes it, or discovers it.
God already sees.
That sounds terrifying.
Until you understand the Gospel.
Because the God who sees what you hide is also the God to whom you can finally stop hiding.
David's story is not simply the story of a wicked man getting what he deserved.
That would be too shallow.
David sinned grievously.
David was confronted.
David repented.
David was forgiven.
And David still experienced devastating temporal consequences.
Those truths belong together.
Listen to David when Nathan confronts him:
חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה
Chatati la-YHWH.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
No speech.
No public-relations campaign.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No blaming stress.
No blaming kingship.
No blaming loneliness.
No rewriting the definition of holiness.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And Nathan responds with extraordinary words:
גַּם־יְהוָה הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ
The LORD has put away David's sin.
That is grace.
But grace did not transform evil into good.
Forgiveness did not mean consequences vanished.
David was forgiven, yet his house still bled.
That distinction matters enormously.
Some people think repentance means saying “sorry” and demanding that every consequence disappear.
Scripture teaches something deeper.
God's forgiveness is real.
God's discipline is real.
God's mercy is real.
And the damage caused by sin can also be painfully real.
You may be forgiven and still need to rebuild trust.
Forgiven and still need accountability.
Forgiven and still need to confess.
Forgiven and still need to repair what you can.
Forgiven and still have scars.
Forgiven and still have people who need time to heal from what you did.
Grace is not God pretending the wreckage never happened.
Grace is God refusing to abandon the repentant sinner in the wreckage.
And there is another uncomfortable part of this story we should not rush past.
The ten women.
After the rebellion was eventually crushed and David returned to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 20:3 tells us what became of them.
David provided for them, but he no longer went in to them, and they lived secluded “in widowhood” until their deaths.
The Bible does not give us their conversations.
It does not record their prayers.
It does not tell us what they felt when Absalom entered Jerusalem or when the tent was raised.
So we should resist filling silence with imagination and calling it Scripture.
But their presence reminds us of something sobering:
Powerful people's sins rarely hurt only powerful people.
Other people get caught in the blast radius.
Children.
Spouses.
Families.
Churches.
Friends.
People whose names never become famous enough to appear in the headline.
That is why repentance cannot merely mean, “God, make me feel better.”
Real repentance asks:
“Lord, what has my sin done?”
“Whom have I wounded?”
“What must I confess?”
“What must I stop?”
“What must I surrender?”
“What needs to change?”
And then comes the question that makes this ancient scandal suddenly personal.
What rooftop are you building?
Maybe yours isn't made of stone.
Maybe yours glows in your hand at two in the morning.
Maybe it is a secret conversation.
Maybe it is resentment rehearsed until hatred feels justified.
Maybe it is pride disguised as ministry.
Maybe it is pornography hidden behind passwords.
Maybe it is emotional infidelity you keep calling friendship.
Maybe it is greed disguised as ambition.
Maybe it is unforgiveness you protect because releasing it feels like letting the person escape justice.
Maybe everyone thinks you are close to Jesus while privately you know you have been drifting for months.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need Christ.
Because eventually the story of David forces us to look beyond David.
David was Israel's king.
But David could not save Israel from sin.
David defeated Goliath but could not defeat the corruption inside his own heart.
David wore a crown but needed mercy.
David wrote psalms but needed forgiveness.
David shepherded a nation but needed a Shepherd himself.
The Bible was preparing us for another King.
Another Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
And look at the contrast.
Absalom wanted his father's throne.
Jesus willingly submitted to His Father.
Absalom exalted himself publicly.
Jesus humbled Himself.
Absalom entered Jerusalem seeking a kingdom through rebellion.
Jesus entered Jerusalem as the rightful King and walked toward a cross.
Absalom's path toward a throne brought shame upon others.
Jesus took our shame upon Himself.
And here the scandal of David's family finally opens toward the scandalous beauty of grace.
David deserved judgment.
So do we.
Yet the Gospel announces that God did not leave sinners without hope.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin's judgment for all who trust in Him.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Not because God suddenly stopped being holy.
Because Christ satisfied what holiness required.
The cross does not tell us that our sin did not matter.
The cross tells us our sin mattered so much that redemption cost the blood of the Son of God.
And the empty tomb tells us sin does not get the final word.
Your scandal does not have to become your final sentence.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your identity.
Your secret does not have to become your master.
Your shame does not have to become your name.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not people with respectable testimonies.
Sinners.
People who have ruined things.
People who knew better.
People who promised God they would never do it again and then did.
People who have carried shame so long they have forgotten what freedom feels like.
People afraid that if anyone really knew them, they would walk away.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to repent and come.
That does not mean, “Continue living however you want because grace will cover it.”
Paul crushes that distortion in Romans 6.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace brings the prodigal home.
Grace turns persecutors into apostles.
Grace transforms the sexually immoral, idolaters, thieves, greedy, drunkards, revilers, and swindlers so Paul can speak of believers and say:
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
That word carries a resurrection inside it.
You may have been that person.
But in Christ, that does not have to be where the sentence ends.
Maybe this article found you while you are still standing on your own secret rooftop.
Come down.
Stop hiding.
Stop negotiating.
Stop saying tomorrow.
Bring the sin into God's light.
Repent.
If another person needs to know, seek godly wisdom and tell the truth appropriately.
Get accountability.
Remove access to whatever repeatedly pulls you back.
Open your Bible again.
Pray even when prayer feels awkward.
Return to fellowship.
And above everything else, fix your eyes on Jesus.
You are not saved because you managed to become impressive enough for God.
You are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
The King who knew every hidden room of your heart loved sinners enough to go to a cross.
And He did not stay dead.
Jesus rose.
That means there is hope for people with histories.
Hope for broken families.
Hope for addicts.
Hope for adulterers who repent.
Hope for hypocrites who finally become honest.
Hope for prodigals.
Hope for the ashamed.
Hope for people whose consequences cannot be completely undone.
Hope even when yesterday cannot be rewritten...
because Jesus can rewrite what happens next.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain Christians with shocking Bible stories.
Not to turn biblical scandal into religious gossip.
But to take people through the difficult pages of Scripture until those pages expose our hearts and point us toward Jesus Christ.
Be honest before God.
Somebody reading beneath this article may need evidence that God still restores broken people.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend whose smile has been hiding a war.
The husband trying to return to God.
The wife carrying silent wounds.
The son who walked away.
The daughter drowning in shame.
The believer who thinks failure has permanently disqualified them.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is for people who have never made a mess of their lives.
Send this article privately if that would be wiser.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and Jesus Christ, supporting and sharing that work is one practical way you can help biblical truth reach another screen, another home, another wounded heart.
Because temptation has a way of making us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
Because somebody else's secret may be killing them quietly.
There are people scrolling Facebook tonight who do not need another argument.
They need to discover that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
David's story began this chapter with a kingdom collapsing.
Absalom turned a rooftop into a monument to rebellion.
A father's hidden sin had produced consequences he could no longer hide.
But neither David's scandal nor Absalom's rebellion would be the final word of Scripture.
Another Son of David was coming.
Another King.
A sinless King.
A King betrayed by people He loved.
A King publicly humiliated.
A King stripped and exposed to shame.
A King crowned with thorns.
A King lifted up before watching crowds.
But unlike David, He was suffering with no secret sin of His own to answer for.
He was the spotless Lamb.
And on the third day...
the grave was empty.
So when the enemy whispers, “Look at what you did,” don't answer by pretending you never did it.
Repent.
Confess.
Then point to Christ.
“Yes. I sinned.
Yes. I need mercy.
Yes. I may carry consequences.
But Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ is still transforming lives.
And my sin will not be greater than my Savior.”
The rooftop may expose the scandal—but the cross reveals how far God was willing to go to redeem the repentant sinner.
